hero.body: Heat, air and noise pollution, housing: Underlaid cross-references these layers to reveal, neighborhood by neighborhood, where exposures stack up across Paris and its inner suburbs — and sets them beside residents' means to cope.

jargon.iris: Neighbourhood: INSEE's statistical division (called IRIS), about 2,000 residents, finer than an arrondissement or a commune.
jargon.quartile: For this criterion, the 2,752 neighbourhoods are split into 4 groups of equal size, from the least affected quarter (1) to the most affected (4).
jargon.cumulativeScore: How many of the 4 categories (heat, air/noise pollution, housing, access to care) place this neighborhood among the most affected quarter of neighborhoods — 0 to 4.
jargon.secondaryResidences: Share of housing units that are secondary residences or occasional dwellings (INSEE, 2022 census) — shown as context, never part of the score. A rough proxy for the ability to physically leave during a heatwave, which median income alone only captures indirectly.
jargon.capacity: Means to cope: a separate axis, never part of the exposure score. Combines median income, housing overcrowding and the share of secondary residences (INSEE: income 2021, 2022 census), ranked across the 2,752 IRIS and split into three equal groups.
jargon.overcrowding: Share of main residences with fewer rooms than the household needs (INSEE definition; one-person studios excluded). In an overcrowded home there's no cooler room to retreat to.
jargon.accessCare: Access to care: the GPs and pharmacies residents can reach without a car (on foot or by public transport), shared among everyone who can reach the same practices and pharmacies. The lower the figure, the weaker the access.
jargon.mobility: Inclusive mobility: the same GP access measure, recomputed for a step-free trip using only the stops and journeys declared wheelchair-accessible. Shown for information, it isn't part of the score: it compares two ways of travelling in the same place, while the score compares places.

ranking.title: Where exposures stack up
ranking.intro: The neighborhoods of Paris and its inner suburbs that are among the most affected quarter of the region's neighborhoods for at least three of the four categories Underlaid tracks — heat, air and noise pollution, energy-inefficient housing, access to care. The four neighborhoods in that position for all four categories come first.
ranking.tieNotice: This isn't a ranking: within a score, the order follows the commune or borough, then the neighborhood name. Position in the list says nothing about how bad one neighborhood's situation is relative to another's.
ranking.footnote: Neighborhoods with fewer than 50 residents (parks, stations, business blocks) stay on the map but are left out of this list. The score moves with each methodological correction and data update: this list isn't final.
ranking.sameScoreNote: Same score, not the same situation. Highly exposed neighborhoods don't face the same exposures depending on their residents' means: where means are highest — mostly dense, older parts of Paris — heat and old, energy-inefficient housing weigh most; where they are lowest — mostly Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne — air and noise pollution, and weaker access to care. So the neighborhoods at 3 out of 4 are grouped by residents' means, measured separately from the score.
ranking.group_low_title: Means among the lowest in the metro area ({n})
ranking.group_low_desc: Residents' means — median income, overcrowded homes, secondary residences (INSEE: income 2021, 2022 census) — are in the metro area's lowest third.
ranking.group_mid_desc: Residents' means are in the metro area's middle third.
ranking.group_high_title: Means among the highest in the metro area ({n})
ranking.group_high_desc: Residents' means are in the metro area's highest third. The exposures are real here too; the map doesn't say which means residents actually use to cope with them.
ranking.group_masked_desc: INSEE doesn't publish income for these small neighborhoods (too few households — statistical secrecy), so they have no means class.
ranking.fig_airNoise: Air and noise index (from 11, the lowest, to 33)
ranking.figuresNote: One figure per category, compared with the metro-wide median. Each category combines several indicators: a figure close to the median doesn't contradict being in the most affected quarter (full detail on the address page).
ranking.group_max_title: In the most affected quarter for all four categories ({n})
ranking.group_max_desc: For heat, air and noise pollution, energy-inefficient housing and access to care, these neighborhoods are among the most affected quarter: the maximum score, 4 out of 4.
ranking.filterEmpty: No neighborhood in this department reaches 3 out of 4.

methodology.title: How the score works
methodology.intro: This page exists so anyone — not just someone comfortable reading code — can check what the map is actually claiming, and where it might be wrong. The full technical version lives in SCORING.md in the project's public repository; this is the same content in plain language.
methodology.countTitle: Why a count, not an average
methodology.countBody1: A single blended average would hide exactly what this project exists to show: neighborhoods where several different problems pile up at once. A neighborhood with one severe problem and two mediocre ones can end up with the same average as a neighborhood with three moderately-bad ones — but those are not the same situation, and a smoothed average can't tell them apart.
methodology.countBody2: So instead of averaging, Underlaid counts: for each neighbourhood, how many of the 4 categories below place it among the most affected quarter of neighbourhoods (the 25% most affected of the 2,752 neighbourhoods of Paris and its inner suburbs for that category). That number, from 0 to 4, is the cumulative score.
methodology.notMeasuredBody1: This is called an exposure score, deliberately not a "vulnerability score." Climate researchers usually split vulnerability into three separate things: exposure (is a place physically subject to heat, pollution, bad housing?), sensitivity (how much does that actually harm the people there — age, health?), and adaptive capacity (can they do something about it — the means to act, a home large enough to find a cooler room, the option to leave during a heatwave?). The exposure score only measures the first one. Adaptive capacity is shown separately (below, and in the map's "Exposure × means" view) and never folded into the score; sensitivity isn't measured.
methodology.notMeasuredBody2: That matters in practice. The income-vs-exposure chart on the map shows that exposure, as measured here, doesn't reliably track income — every score band spans nearly the whole income range, including several of the metro area's wealthiest neighborhoods. A wealthy household facing the same physical exposure (heat, noise, an old apartment) usually has more ways to cope with it than a low-income one does. Two neighborhoods can share the exact same score and still face very different real odds of coping — which is precisely why this page never calls that score "vulnerability."
methodology.notMeasuredBody3: The ranking page's split into "Group A" and "Group B" exists for the same reason: it keeps a lower-income neighborhood with a real service shortfall visually distinct from a wealthier one whose score comes from dense, older housing stock instead — same exposure score, different starting point for coping with it.
methodology.subscoresIntro: Every category is built from several raw indicators, each converted to "how exposed" so they combine consistently, then averaged together with equal weight — there isn't yet a principled reason to consider one indicator more important than another.
methodology.thermalDesc: Heat vulnerability index, how many cool facilities (pools, museums, libraries) sit within 400m, how much of the neighborhood is covered by open green/wooded space, and the share of its surface that's artificialized/sealed — built or paved ground holds and re-radiates heat rather than absorbing it.
methodology.pollutionDesc: Combined air pollution and noise exposure class, area-weighted across the neighborhood.
methodology.housingDesc: Share of sampled housing energy-performance certificates rated F or G — France's official "thermal sieve" categories, homes that are expensive and uncomfortable to heat or cool — combined with how sharply a neighborhood's residential electricity use swings with winter temperature (Enedis), a proxy for electric-heating-dependent homes with no cheap way to compensate for heat either.
methodology.thresholdTitle: The "not enough data" rule — and the bias it fixed
methodology.thresholdBody1: A category is only scored for a neighborhood if data exists for a strict majority of its underlying indicators. Below that, the category is marked "insufficient data" for that neighborhood and left out of its cumulative score entirely — never silently treated as "fine" or averaged from whatever scraps happened to be available.
methodology.thresholdBody2: This rule exists because of a real bias found in the original Paris-only data, not a hypothetical one. Two small, non-residential neighborhoods — a Périphérique interchange and a dense commercial block near a department store — were scoring the maximum at the time (4 out of 4, when access to services was still counted), driven partly by an "access" category built from just one or two of its four indicators. Checked across all 992 Paris neighborhoods: among those whose access category relied on a single indicator, 47% landed among the most affected quarter, nearly double the 25% you'd expect by chance. Sparse-data neighborhoods were being penalized for lacking data, not for having worse access.
methodology.thresholdBody3: After the fix, both of those examples dropped out of the top score — and the same kind of bias, found again in a milder form at launch, took the earlier access indicators out of the score, before access came back in a rebuilt form (see below).
methodology.electricalBody1: Housing originally used one indicator: the share of homes rated F or G on energy performance. A neighborhood can now also be flagged by how sharply its residential electricity use swings with winter temperature (data from Enedis, the grid operator) — a proxy for electric-heating-dependent homes with no cheap way to compensate for heat either, not just cold.
methodology.electricalBody2: Both indicators are now required, not just one — a real tightening, not a bug. The two Paris examples above moved again as a result (to 2 out of 4 at the time): both still had enough housing data, but their thermosensitivity turned out close to the citywide average rather than among the most affected quarter, which took their housing category out of that quarter.
methodology.expansionTitle: Expanding beyond Paris — and a new example
methodology.expansionBody1: Underlaid covers the whole inner ring of the Greater Paris metropolis: Paris, Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne, 2,752 neighbourhoods instead of 992. Most sources were already national or regional. Two heat indicators (cool places, cool green space) existed for Paris only: they were replaced by regional sources (the public inventory of pools, museums and libraries, and a regional survey of green and wooded areas), applied the same way everywhere.
methodology.expansionBody2: A fourth heat indicator was added at the same time: the share of each neighbourhood's surface that is sealed (built or paved, from the regional land-use survey), a structural cause of heat retention. Two Paris-only context facts (tree age, street lighting) have no regional equivalent and stay flagged as Paris-only; associational density had one and covers the 143 communes.
methodology.expansionBody3: 4 neighborhoods currently reach the maximum, 4 out of 4: Flachat I in Asnières-sur-Seine, Nonneville 3 and 4 in Aulnay-sous-Bois, Quatre Cités 3 in Champigny-sur-Marne. 81 inhabited neighborhoods reach 3 out of 4 or more, spread across Paris (22), Hauts-de-Seine (23), Seine-Saint-Denis (18) and Val-de-Marne (18); they are listed on the ranking page. Any example on this page is provisional — the score moves with each methodological correction.
methodology.expansionBody4: This same territory already has a regional precedent worth naming directly: ORS Île-de-France, Ineris and L'Institut Paris Region published "Cumuls d'expositions environnementales en Île-de-France" (2022), a 5-year, 500m-grid study of composite exposure across the whole region, including a case study on Aubervilliers — a commune inside this project's own coverage. It confirms the same underlying idea from an independent source: environmental burdens in this region do stack up in identifiable places. Underlaid's own difference is granularity (IRIS rather than a 500m grid) and a count of the least favourable categories rather than a blended index (see "About" on the home page for the full comparison).
methodology.limitsIntro: Naming these limits openly is what makes the score checkable — hiding them would only delay the moment someone else finds them.
methodology.limitIncome: Median income is masked by INSEE for small neighborhoods (privacy threshold): 223 of 2,752 have no published figure. Income is shown for context only — it is never part of the score.
methodology.limitIcu: The heat vulnerability index covers 2,618 of 2,752 neighborhoods; the source dataset uses a slightly coarser grouping that misses full coverage. The other heat indicators (cool facilities, green area, artificialization) do cover all 2,752.
methodology.limitThermosensitivity: Electrical thermosensitivity is a winter-heating signal — Enedis doesn't publish a summer-cooling equivalent. Using it as a proxy for "can't compensate for heat" assumes a poorly-insulated, electric-heating-dependent home is also hard to keep cool, which is physically reasonable but not independently checked against real summer electricity data.
methodology.limitArtificialization: The artificialized-surface classification (54 of 79 land-use categories) is modeled closely on France's official artificialisation definition but isn't a certified reproduction of it — there's no single published crosswalk from this specific regional land-use legend to the legal nomenclature. It also doubles as a rough urban-biodiversity signal — sealed ground is lost habitat — though it isn't scored separately for wildlife, since no animal mortality or stress data comparable to what's available for humans exists at this grain.
methodology.limitEstimate: The score is an estimate, not a fixed ground truth. Every methodological correction moves the line — treat any single flagship example as provisional until checked against the raw indicators, the way every example on this page was.
methodology.distNote: 4 neighborhoods currently reach 4 out of 4 and 79 others 3 out of 4 (81 inhabited in all). Treat them as provisional evidence, not a settled verdict: the score moves with each methodological correction.
methodology.distLastUpdated: Data snapshot as of {date} — the score is re-computed periodically and can shift; a specific example above should always be read against this date, not treated as permanent.
methodology.licensesIntro: Everything here is built from public open data. Each source keeps its own license, checked against what the publisher itself states. Underlaid's code is under the MIT license; the published data (the score and every indicator behind it) is under the Open Database License (ODbL), because two sources — OpenStreetMap and the Ville de Paris datasets — are ODbL, which requires derived data to be shared under the same terms.
methodology.licensesNote: Mandatory citations — INSEE: "Source: Insee". Air-noise map: "Source des données : Cartographie air-bruit établie par Airparif et Bruitparif – http://carto.airparif.bruitparif.fr". OpenStreetMap: "© OpenStreetMap contributors". Transport timetables: "Contains information from ‘Horaires prévus sur les lignes de transport en commun d'Île-de-France (GTFS Datahub)’, made available by Île-de-France Mobilités under the terms of the ‘Licence Mobilités’." To cite Underlaid, see the repository's CITATION.cff file, and state the data snapshot date (shown at the bottom of every page).
methodology.capacityTitle: Means to cope: a separate axis
methodology.capacityBody1: The map's "Exposure × means" view crosses the exposure score with a second, separate measure: the means residents have to cope. It combines three INSEE figures (income 2021, 2022 census): median income, the share of overcrowded homes (fewer rooms than the household needs — no cooler room to retreat to), and the share of secondary residences (the option to leave during a heatwave). Each neighborhood is ranked on each figure, the three ranks are averaged, and the 2,752 neighborhoods are split into three equal groups: lowest, middle and highest third of the metro area.
methodology.capacityBody2: It is never added to the exposure score. Kept apart, the two can be read side by side: two neighborhoods with the same exposure can have very different means to cope with it. INSEE doesn't publish income for 223 small neighborhoods (mostly woods, parks and business areas); they have no means class and are shown as such, never estimated.
methodology.capacityBody3: What it shows: highly exposed neighborhoods don't face the same exposures depending on their means. Those with the highest means are mostly in Paris and stack heat and old, inefficient housing; those with the lowest means are mostly in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne and stack mainly heat, air pollution and noise. Overall, the link between exposure and means is weak — and slightly positive only because of dense, older central Paris; in the three inner-suburb departments there's almost no link. Where high exposure and low means do meet, it's concentrated: in Seine-Saint-Denis, 62% of highly exposed neighborhoods (at least 2 of the 3 exposures: heat, air and noise, housing) are in the metro area's lowest third of means; in Paris, 4.5%.
methodology.capacityBody4: What it doesn't show: it measures means, not what households do with them — nothing here says whether a home has air conditioning or whether someone can take time off during a heatwave. The groups are relative to this metro area, not an absolute threshold of "enough."
methodology.accessOutTitle: Access to care: taken out, rebuilt, back in the score
methodology.accessOut1: At launch, the score counted a fourth category, access to services. Crossing the score with residents' means showed it wasn't measuring what it claimed, and a series of checks confirmed it for each of its four indicators. It was taken out of the score in September 2026, then rebuilt; those earlier indicators stay on display for information in the detail panel.
methodology.accessOut2: The social position index of nearby schools reflected families' resources, already measured separately on the means axis: keeping it in the score counted them twice. It accounted for most of the link between the access category and residents' means (correlation −0.52).
methodology.accessOut3: Wheelchair-accessible entrances come from a crowdsourced register, missing for 39% of neighbourhoods. Neighbourhoods without it landed in the least well-served quarter 29.6% of the time, against 17.6% for the others: the same missing-data bias the project had already corrected once.
methodology.accessOut4: Pedestrian-path density, from OpenStreetMap, mostly measures how volunteers map sidewalks: Paris draws 53% of its sidewalks as separate paths, Seine-Saint-Denis 17% — elsewhere they're usually noted as an attribute of the street, which wasn't counted. Checked on aerial imagery: the "Klock" neighborhood in Clichy (53,000 residents per km², sidewalks clearly visible) counted 52 m of path per km²; Saint-Ambroise 4 in Paris's 11th, with the same kind of streets, 165,000.
methodology.accessOut5: Travel time to the nearest school, clinic or transport stop is 1.5 minutes or less for 98% of neighborhoods in this dense area, so it barely tells them apart. Hence the rebuild: a measure that accounts for how many people share each service, not just how close it is.
methodology.thresholdBody4: The thresholds that delimit the most affected quarter are set from inhabited neighbourhoods only. The 62 neighborhoods with fewer than 50 residents — parks, river banks, rail yards, stations, business blocks — are placed against those thresholds afterwards: they keep a score on the map, marked "very sparsely populated", but they no longer take up places in the most affected quarter that belong to neighbourhoods where people live. 74% of them were among the most affected quarter for air and noise, since they often sit along rail lines and expressways.
methodology.sidewalkTitle: Sidewalks in OpenStreetMap: counted properly, still uneven
methodology.sidewalkBody1: To see whether the pedestrian figure could be repaired, sidewalks were counted both ways OpenStreetMap records them — drawn as separate lines, or noted on the street itself (sidewalk=both/left/right) — each sidewalk counted once. That fixes the Klock example: 1.87 m of sidewalk per metre of street, against 1.76 in Saint-Ambroise 4. But the deeper problem remains: for many streets OpenStreetMap says nothing about sidewalks at all, and how often depends on the department, even between neighborhoods of the same density.
methodology.sidewalkCaption: Share of street length with any sidewalk information in OpenStreetMap (extract of September 30, 2026), by population density of the neighborhood
methodology.sidewalkNote: Density bands are fifths of the inhabited neighborhoods (50 residents or more). * Fewer than 20 neighborhoods of that department in the band.
methodology.sidewalkBody2: Unknown doesn't mean absent: in Firmin Gemier (Aubervilliers), OpenStreetMap records no sidewalk on any street, while aerial imagery shows them. What matters in a wheelchair is recorded even less evenly: sidewalk width for under 1% of sidewalks everywhere; surface for 72% in Paris and 21% in Seine-Saint-Denis; kerbs about 119 times per 100 pedestrian crossings in Paris, 33 in Seine-Saint-Denis.
methodology.sidewalkBody3: Conclusion: no sidewalk figure from OpenStreetMap can compare neighborhoods across departments. The rule, set before computing, allowed a gap of at most 15 points between departments at equal density; the gap reaches 71 points. So none enters the score, and the old footway density no longer appears on the map. Access to services will be rebuilt from official sources (Île-de-France Mobilités accessibility data, health directories), with walking routed on the full street network rather than on sidewalks.
methodology.carFreeTitle: The access measure: without a car
methodology.carFreeBody1: Access to care is measured with a method that shares each service's capacity among everyone who can reach it, not just the distance to the nearest one. It counts what residents can reach on foot and by public transport, not by car. That choice follows from what Underlaid is about: equal access to everyday services for everyone, including people who can't drive or don't have a car — children and teenagers, many older people, people with disabilities or a pushchair, and the many households without a car in dense areas.
methodology.carFreeBody2: So a neighborhood where doctors are easy to reach by car but far on foot or by bus ranks low on this measure: that's what it's meant to show. It is also why it differs from the official DREES indicator (APL), which uses car travel times between communes. The two answer different questions.
methodology.accessCareDesc: The GPs and pharmacies residents can reach without a car, on foot or by public transport, taking into account everyone who can reach the same practices and pharmacies (a "floating catchment area" method, the same family as the DREES APL indicator). GPs: up to 20 minutes, with a weight that decreases beyond 10 minutes; pharmacies: a 15-minute walk.
methodology.accessBackTitle: How access to care was rebuilt
methodology.accessBack1: Liberal GPs and GPs employed by health centres (RPPS directory, the same field as the DREES APL indicator) and pharmacies (FINESS), shared among the population of each 200 m square (INSEE, 2021), weighted by age with the DREES weights. Travel times are computed on foot and by public transport on the OpenStreetMap street network and the Île-de-France Mobilités timetables, for a Tuesday between 10:00 and 11:00. The whole of Île-de-France is included, so neighborhoods on the edge of the inner ring also see services across the boundary.
methodology.accessBack2: Structures without local, everyday consultations were left out after checking by hand every address with at least 15 GPs: teleconsultation platforms, on-call and home-visit services, hospital emergency departments, services reserved to one population (students, airports). The list, with the reason for each exclusion, is published in SCORING.md.
methodology.accessBack3: Before crossing this measure with residents' means, the hypothesis and its criteria were written down and dated: are neighborhoods with the lowest means at a disadvantage in access to care, clearly and in several departments? Result: yes. In both Hauts-de-Seine and Val-de-Marne, about 41% of neighborhoods in the lowest third of means are in the least-served quarter of neighborhoods, against 24% in the highest third; at equal population density, the gap reaches 23 points. Seine-Saint-Denis couldn't be assessed by the rule set in advance: only one of its neighborhoods is in the metro area's highest third of means.
methodology.mobilityBody1: The same measure was recomputed for a wheelchair trip: step-free, using only the stops and journeys declared accessible. The hypothesis doesn't hold for this measure: the loss of access doesn't weigh more on the neighborhoods with the lowest means. Metro inaccessibility mostly penalises wheelchair journeys within Paris, whatever the neighbourhood's level of resources. Counted in GPs within reach, wheelchair access remains lower in the inner suburbs.
methodology.mobilityBody2: It is shown in the detail panel but isn't part of the score: it compares two ways of travelling in the same place, while the score compares places. That decision was made after seeing the crossing with residents' means; it doesn't change the result above.

press.title: Underlaid — press kit
press.subtitle: One-page summary of the methodology, for citation without a follow-up call.
press.whatBody: Underlaid maps cumulative environmental exposure across 2,752 neighbourhoods of Paris and its inner suburbs (INSEE's IRIS division, about 2,000 residents each; Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, Val-de-Marne): for each one, the number of categories (heat, air pollution and noise, housing, access to care) on which it is among the most affected quarter of neighbourhoods. A count from 0 to 4, not an average, set beside residents' means, measured separately.
press.countTitle: Why a count, not an average
press.countBody: A blended average would hide neighborhoods that stack several distinct problems at once — exactly what this project exists to show. Counting, instead of smoothing, keeps that distinction visible.
press.thermalLine: Heat — heat vulnerability index, nearby cool places, cool green space, share of sealed ground.
press.pollutionLine: Air pollution and noise — combined exposure to air pollution and noise (Airparif and Bruitparif map).
press.housingLine: Housing — share of homes rated F or G on energy performance, combined with residential electrical thermosensitivity (Enedis).
press.caveat1: Income is shown for context only, never part of the score (INSEE masks 223 of 2,752 neighborhoods for privacy).
press.caveat2: The heat vulnerability index covers 2,618 of 2,752 neighbourhoods; the other heat indicators cover all 2,752.
press.caveat3: Inclusive mobility (GP access in a wheelchair) is shown for information, not scored: it compares two ways of travelling in the same place. Metro inaccessibility mostly penalises wheelchair journeys within Paris, whatever the neighbourhood's level of resources; counted in GPs within reach, wheelchair access remains lower in the inner suburbs.
press.caveat4: The score is an estimate that shifts with each methodological correction, not a fixed ranking — access to services left the count at launch (score out of 3), then came back in a rebuilt form, access to care (score out of 4, version 0.2, October 2026).
press.sourceLine: Full methodology and caveats: see SCORING.md in the project documentation.
press.dataSources: Data: INSEE · IGN · CSTB · L'Institut Paris Region · Airparif/Bruitparif ("Cartographie air-bruit établie par Airparif et Bruitparif – http://carto.airparif.bruitparif.fr") · ADEME · Enedis · ANS (RPPS) · FINESS · DREES · Île-de-France Mobilités · IGN BD TOPO · DEPP · Acceslibre · Ville de Paris · © OpenStreetMap contributors. Licence Ouverte 2.0, ODbL and Licence Mobilités — published data under ODbL, code under MIT. Full list: methodology page, "Data sources & licenses".
press.meansTitle: Means to cope — a separate axis
press.meansBody: The exposure score doesn't say who can cope. A second, separate measure does: median income, overcrowded homes and secondary residences (INSEE: income 2021, 2022 census), ranked and split into thirds of the metro area. It is never added to the score; the map's "Exposure × means" view crosses the two. Highly exposed areas with the most means are mostly in Paris (heat, old housing); those with the least are mostly in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne (heat, air and noise). In Seine-Saint-Denis, 62% of highly exposed neighborhoods (at least 2 of the 3 exposures) are in the lowest third of means; in Paris, 4.5%. It measures means, not what households do with them (e.g. air conditioning).
press.accessCareLine: Access to care — GPs and pharmacies reachable without a car, on foot or by public transport, shared among everyone who can reach them.
press.idfmNotice: Contains information from "Horaires prévus sur les lignes de transport en commun d'Île-de-France (GTFS Datahub)", made available by Île-de-France Mobilités under the terms of the "Licence Mobilités".

about.intro: Underlaid didn't invent this idea — it borrows from tools that came before it, and exists inside an active policy debate. Naming both openly is part of being checkable.
about.orsInerisTitle: ORS Île-de-France / Ineris / L'Institut Paris Region, 2022
about.orsInerisBody: "Cumuls d'expositions environnementales en Île-de-France": a 5-year, 500m-grid regional study of composite environmental exposure across the whole of Île-de-France, with a public interactive map and a case study on Aubervilliers — a commune inside Underlaid's own Métropole du Grand Paris coverage. The most directly comparable regional precedent found: same core idea (composite exposure, not a single index), a coarser and non-cumulative grid rather than a neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood count of the least favourable categories.
about.orsInerisSource: Source: ORS Île-de-France, Ineris, L'Institut Paris Region, 2022 — interactive map at cartoviz.institutparisregion.fr.
about.adaptBody: The closest existing French tool: 137 agglomerations, focused on officially recognized priority neighborhoods (QPV), built on a 200m grid. Underlaid's difference: IRIS-level granularity (finer than QPV), a public interactive map rather than an institutional report, and a cumulative count rather than a smoothed average.
about.ejBody: US environmental-justice screening tools (federal EPA, California, New York City) that pioneered composite cumulative-burden scoring at small-area granularity. Underlaid adapts the same core idea — count how many burdens stack up in the same place, don't average them away — to Paris and to a different set of indicators.
about.hccTitle: Haut Conseil pour le Climat, July 9, 2026 report
about.hccBody: "France isn't ready": the report that coined "bouilloires thermiques" (thermal kettles) for the worst-affected neighborhoods, published as the state cut the Fonds Vert budget from €2.5bn to €837M and the idea of a "service public de la fraîcheur" (public cooling service) entered debate. Underlaid is built to make that debate concrete at the scale of an actual street.
about.hccSource: Source: Haut Conseil pour le Climat, press coverage, 2026-07-09.

context.intro: Six facts that are not counted in the score, because they are only available at a coarser scale than the neighbourhood (arrondissement, commune, region). They are shown as context. Three concern Paris only (flagged below): no equivalent source exists yet for the inner suburbs.
context.lifeExpectancyBody: The 5th, 6th, 7th and 16th arrondissements are among the highest life expectancies in the Paris agglomeration (84+ years). The 18th, 19th, 20th and 10th arrondissements — denser, lower-income — range 79.9-80.9 years (men) / 85.4-85.6 years (women). No equivalent figure was found for the inner-suburb communes.
context.lifeExpectancySource: Source: Institut Paris Région / APUR, ORS Île-de-France.
context.heatwaveBody: in Île-de-France, June 22-28, 2026 — a national record for that week, per Santé publique France's official count. This figure already covers the whole region, Paris and inner suburbs alike; no finer breakdown exists.
context.heatwaveSource: Source: Santé publique France, press release, 2026-06-27.
context.schoolsTitle: Air-conditioned schools during the June 2026 heatwave (Paris only)
context.schoolsBody: Plan announced on 20 June 2026 by the City of Paris: more than 1,200 portable air conditioners ordered for 620 schools. Figures by arrondissement were published for only 8 of 20 arrondissements; they were collected from the press and from the arrondissement town halls' websites. No equivalent information was found for the inner suburbs.
context.schoolsSource: Source: arrondissement mairies / local press, compiled 2026-07-11 — see scripts/16_school_ac_context.py.
context.treesTitle: How old is the street canopy (Paris only)
context.treesBody: There's no public planting-date record for Paris's ~219,000 street trees, so trunk circumference (the standard arboriculture proxy — wider means older) stands in instead. The spread is real: {lowName} averages just {lowCm}cm, against {highCm}cm in {highName} — a rough proxy for how long each arrondissement's tree canopy has actually been growing, not just how much of it there is today. Paris's own tree inventory has no inner-suburb equivalent, so this stays Paris-only.
context.treesRow: {cm}cm average circumference, {young} still young saplings ({n} trees recorded)
context.treesSource: Source: Ville de Paris, "Arbres" dataset (opendata.paris.fr), aggregated by arrondissement.
context.lightingBody: A nighttime-visibility proxy only — not a measure of actual safety or crime. {lowName} has the lowest density at {lowDensity} lamps/km², against {highDensity} lamps/km² in {highName}. Paris's own lighting inventory has no inner-suburb equivalent, so this stays Paris-only.
context.lightingSource: Source: Ville de Paris, "eclairage public" dataset (opendata.paris.fr), aggregated by arrondissement.
context.rnaBody: How many currently-active associations are headquartered per 1,000 residents in each commune, from the national register (RNA) — now covering all 143 communes of Paris and the inner suburbs, not just Paris's 20 arrondissements. {lowName} has the lowest rate at {lowRate}/1,000, against {highRate}/1,000 in {highName}.
context.rnaCaveat: Reported per 1,000 residents as the primary figure; per km² is shown alongside since it's a separate, real distortion that per-capita alone doesn't fix — the lowest-density-per-km² communes include the Bois de Vincennes and Bois de Boulogne, whose large park area alone pulls that figure down, not necessarily weaker associational life. A headquarters address also isn't where an association's members live or its activity happens. Read this as one data point, not a verdict on civic health.
context.rnaSource: Source: Repertoire National des Associations, Ile-de-France mirror (data.iledefrance.fr), aggregated by commune; population from the INSEE 2022 census.
context.layerAsOf: Data as of {date}: the latest refresh of this source failed, so its previous version is shown.

bivariate.intro: Each neighborhood is placed on two separate axes: how exposed it is (the cumulative score, grouped as 0, 1, or 2 and more) and the means its residents have to cope (lowest, middle or highest third of the metro area). The exposure score itself doesn't change.
bivariate.masked: Income not published: few or no residents (statistical secrecy)
bivariate.caption: Darkest = exposures stacked and among the lowest means
bivariate.cell_0_0: None of the 4 categories among the most affected quarter, with among the lowest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_0_1: None of the 4 categories among the most affected quarter, with middle-range means.
bivariate.cell_0_2: None of the 4 categories among the most affected quarter, with among the highest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_1_0: One category among the most affected quarter, with among the lowest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_1_1: One category among the most affected quarter, with middle-range means.
bivariate.cell_1_2: One category among the most affected quarter, with among the highest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_2_0: At least two categories among the most affected quarter, with among the lowest means in the metro area: the combination where making up for the exposure with one's own means is hardest.
bivariate.cell_2_1: At least two categories among the most affected quarter, with middle-range means.
bivariate.cell_2_2: At least two categories among the most affected quarter, with among the highest means in the metro area. The exposure is real; the map doesn't say which means residents actually use to cope with it.

method.title: Sources and method
method.lead: All the data comes from public sources and can be checked. This page sets out the essentials; the detailed method and the code are published.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.intro: The data comes from public bodies and open databases. It is downloaded again at every quarterly update, except access to care, which is recomputed by hand.
sources.legend: Flagged: a more recent edition exists but is not used, or does not exist at neighbourhood level. The reason is given.
sources.mobilityNotice: Contains information from "Horaires prévus sur les lignes de transport en commun d'Île-de-France (GTFS Datahub)", made available by Île-de-France Mobilités under the terms of the "Licence Mobilités".

rows.who: French digital health agency (RPPS); Ministry of Health (FINESS)

rows.note: 2023 edition published at commune level only, with a changed method: not comparable.

2022 edition, reference since 3 October 2026. INSEE changes the definition of overcrowding in it: the median rate goes from 13.5% to 24.6%, with no real change. The differences with 2021 are published as a sensitivity check.

calc.title: How the score is calculated
calc.intro: Paris and its inner suburbs are divided into 2,752 neighbourhoods, following INSEE's official division (about 2,000 residents each). Four criteria are assessed for each.

criteria.name: Heat
criteria.desc: Heat vulnerability, sealed ground, cool green spaces, cool places within 400 metres.

criteria.name: Air pollution and noise
criteria.desc: Combined exposure to air pollution and noise, from the Airparif and Bruitparif map.

criteria.name: Housing
criteria.desc: Share of homes rated F or G, and how strongly electricity consumption rises with the cold.

criteria.name: Access to care
criteria.desc: GPs and pharmacies reachable on foot or by public transport, relative to the number of residents who can also reach them.

calc.resultDesc: A criterion is unfavourable when the neighbourhood is among the most affected quarter of neighbourhoods. Score from 0 to 4.
calc.countNotMean: The score is a count, not an average. An average smooths differences away: a very hot but quiet neighbourhood would get the same mark as a moderately hot, moderately noisy one. Counting shows the neighbourhoods where difficulties add up.
calc.distSources: Underlaid calculation from the sources above

measures.title: Four measures, published separately
measures.intro: The score does not sum everything up. Four measures are published for each neighbourhood; only the first two enter the score.

items.name: Environmental exposure
items.desc: Heat, air pollution and noise, housing: the three exposures measured.

items.name: Access to care
items.desc: GPs and pharmacies reachable without a car, taking into account how many people share each practice or pharmacy.

items.name: Residents' means
items.status: Measured separately, never in the score
items.desc: Median income, share of overcrowded homes, share of second homes. Crossing it with exposure shows whether the two coincide, without assuming it.

items.name: Inclusive mobility
items.status: Published for information, outside the score
items.desc: Share of GP access kept when travelling step-free (wheelchair, pushchair). It compares two ways of travelling from the same place, not places with each other.

items.name: Individual situations.
items.desc: The indicators describe neighbourhoods, not the age, health or circumstances of their residents.

items.name: Private adaptations.
items.desc: Air conditioning, shutters or private solutions do not appear in public data.

items.name: Risks not included.
items.desc: Flooding, soil pollution and industrial risks are not yet taken into account.

items.name: A relative score.
items.desc: Neighbourhoods are compared with each other: adding data can change the results.

items.name: Step-free travel.
items.desc: Step-free times and access are a lower bound: the calculation avoids stairs and stops declared inaccessible, but accounts neither for lifts out of order, nor pavement condition, nor a slower speed, nor whether the destination building is accessible.

items.name: Access to care.
items.desc: Each GP counts as one, whatever their working hours: each practitioner's actual activity is not public.

items.name: Public toilets and water points.
items.desc: Only the City of Paris publishes a complete list (toilets and fountains). In the inner suburbs, partial lists exist but cover only a few communes: Grand Paris Seine Ouest (173 fountains and 33 toilets, for 7 communes), Sceaux (21 fountains), Montreuil (22 fountains, 2019 list); Seine-Saint-Denis publishes an OpenStreetMap extract (271 water points) of unknown completeness. These places are therefore shown for Paris neighbourhoods only.

fixes.title: Corrections made
fixes.intro: Indicators that measured something other than what they were meant to measure were removed, including when they widened the observed gaps.

items.what: Access to services removed from the score, pending a reliable measure
items.why: The data measured distance to services rather than their capacity, and was incomplete in the inner suburbs.
Pavement information exists for 96% of street length in Paris but 26% in Seine-Saint-Denis: no fair comparison was possible.

items.what: Nearly uninhabited neighbourhoods excluded from the thresholds
items.why: Neighbourhoods with fewer than 50 residents (river banks, parks, business areas) skewed the comparison thresholds.

items.what: Energy ratings of small homes checked
items.why: The labels published by ADEME already include the 2024 correction for homes under 40 m²: no adjustment needed.

items.what: Access to care: structures without on-site consultations excluded
items.why: Teleconsultation platforms, SOS Médecins, emergency departments: list published, with the reason for each exclusion.

items.what: Access to care back in the score
items.why: Rebuilt measure: the capacity of GPs and pharmacies shared among the residents who can reach them on foot or by public transport.

Population, overcrowded homes and second homes move from the 2021 to the 2022 census; income stays 2021, the latest vintage published at neighbourhood level. The site's key figures are updated. The hypotheses' verdicts, computed on 2021, remain the official results and are checked with 2022. Overcrowding changes definition at INSEE (median rate from 13.5% to 24.6%, with no real change).

home.title: One city, unequal living conditions.
home.lead: Heat, air pollution and noise, housing, access to care: the gaps between neighbourhoods, measured from public data.
home.hint: The main findings are set out below.

f1.title: {n} neighbourhoods are among the most affected on all four criteria at once.
f1.body: Heat, air pollution and noise, energy-inefficient housing, access to care: these are usually mapped separately. How they overlap, neighbourhood by neighbourhood, rarely is.
f1.body2: {n} inhabited neighbourhoods are among the most affected quarter on at least three of the four criteria.
f1.alt: Map of Paris and its inner suburbs: each neighbourhood is shaded by the number of criteria on which it is among the most affected quarter, from 0 (light pink) to 4 (dark red).
f1.legend: Number of criteria on which the neighbourhood is among the most affected quarter
f1.sources: CSTB, L'Institut Paris Region, INSEE, Airparif and Bruitparif, ADEME, Enedis, ANS, Île-de-France Mobilités

f2.title: Same exposure, opposite social situations.
f2.body: Among highly exposed neighbourhoods whose residents have the most means, most are in Paris and combine mainly heat and energy-inefficient housing. Among those whose residents have the fewest means, most are in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne, and combine mainly heat, air pollution and noise.
f2.body2: Across the metropolis, the link between exposure and means is weak (rank correlation {rho}), and slightly positive because of central Paris, dense and old.
f2.question: Among highly exposed neighbourhoods (at least 2 of the 3 exposures), what share is also in the metro area's third where residents have the fewest means?
f2.definition: The 3 exposures: heat, air pollution and noise, housing. Access to care is measured separately. Residents' means: median income, share of overcrowded homes, share of second homes (INSEE: income 2021, 2022 census), measured separately from the score.
f2.sources: INSEE, CSTB, Airparif and Bruitparif, ADEME

quiz.question: Where is the share of wheelchair-accessible metro stop points highest?
quiz.explanation: Seine-Saint-Denis: {ssd} of metro stop points marked wheelchair-accessible. Paris: {paris}. In Seine-Saint-Denis, they are the stop points of the recent extensions of lines 11 and 14.

f3.title: Access to care also depends on how many people share what is on offer.
f3.body: Number of GPs and pharmacies reachable on foot or by public transport, relative to all the residents who can also reach them. In Hauts-de-Seine and Val-de-Marne, neighbourhoods whose residents have the fewest means are more often among the least well served.
f3.question: Share of neighbourhoods among the least well-served quarter for care, by residents' means
f3.density: At equal population density, the gap reaches {n92} points in Hauts-de-Seine and {n94} points in Val-de-Marne (test set before any calculation, October 2026). In Seine-Saint-Denis, almost no neighbourhood is in the third with the most means: no comparison is possible.
f3.wheelchair: In a wheelchair, the number of GPs within reach remains lower in the inner suburbs: median of {p} per 10,000 residents in Paris, {d92} in Hauts-de-Seine, {d93} in Seine-Saint-Denis, {d94} in Val-de-Marne. This is a lower bound: lifts out of order, pavement condition and a slower speed are not taken into account.
f3.sources: ANS (RPPS), FINESS, INSEE, Île-de-France Mobilités, OpenStreetMap

f4.title: Public data that is uneven from one area to another.
f4.body: Pavements are recorded by OpenStreetMap's volunteer contributors. This record is almost complete in Paris and patchy in Seine-Saint-Denis: missing data does not mean there is no pavement. This data was therefore left out of the calculation.

hypotheses.intro: Before looking at the results, the hypotheses to test were written down and dated, with the rule that decides the verdict. This avoids looking, after the fact, for the story the figures seem to tell.

care.statement: Neighbourhoods whose residents have the fewest means have more difficult access to care.
care.result: True in Hauts-de-Seine and Val-de-Marne, including at comparable density. The rule fixed in advance does not allow a conclusion in Seine-Saint-Denis, where almost no neighbourhood is in the metropolis's third with the most means.
care.control: The quarter with the most difficult access to care holds {d92l} of the neighbourhoods with the fewest means against {d92h} of those with the most in Hauts-de-Seine, {d94l} against {d94h} in Val-de-Marne; gap over the metropolis {mgpGap} points (29.4 with the 2021 census).

wheelchair.statement: Neighbourhoods whose residents have the fewest means lose more access to care in a wheelchair.
wheelchair.result: No: the loss of access in a wheelchair is concentrated in Paris, where few metro stop points are accessible, whatever the neighbourhood's means. In number of reachable GPs, wheelchair access remains lower in the inner suburbs.
wheelchair.control: The loss of access in a wheelchair remains concentrated in Paris ({d75l} of the neighbourhoods with the fewest means in the most affected quarter, against {d75h} of those with the most); over the metropolis, {mgpl} against {mgph}.

publicServices.statement: Neighbourhoods whose residents have the fewest means are more often far from public services (town hall, France Services, CAF, CPAM, France Travail, post office).
publicServices.result: The reverse holds in Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne, and the result is the same in a wheelchair.
publicServices.tableCaption: Share of neighbourhoods in the quarter farthest from public services (on foot and by public transport, Tuesday 10:00), by residents' means. Thirds of means computed within each département.
publicServices.after: Neighbourhoods with the most means are more often far from public services, including at comparable density in Hauts-de-Seine and Val-de-Marne. The data do not establish why.
publicServices.caveat: This indicator measures travel time on foot and by public transport. It does not take into account the need to use these services, car use or online procedures.

how.title: How are these durations computed?
how.free: Walking at 4.5 km/h, on the whole public transport network.
how.slow: Same network, but walking at 3.4 km/h on every walking part: from home, to the stop, in connections and to the destination. It is the usual walking speed measured in people aged 80 and over (Bohannon and Andrews, 2011). This profile can also give an idea of a trip with pain, late in pregnancy or with a young child walking alongside.
how.wheelchair: Only stops and stations declared step-free are used. The calculation sees neither pavements, slopes, broken lifts nor the help sometimes needed to board a train: real durations are often longer.
how.all: All durations: departure on a Tuesday at 10:00 (at night: 1:00), real timetables, median over the time window.
